title: Goal Settings
summary:
Setting goals defines the direction of an exercise program, makes results measurable and raises adherence. Goals should be clear, individualized, evidence-based, and can target safety and prevention, functional optimization, metabolic and cardiovascular health, psychological well-being and preparation for childbirth. The chapter adapts the SMART model to pregnancy, for example raising the 30-s chair stand test from 10 to 14 repetitions.

Adherence is limited by physical, psychological and social factors, so the chapter applies four motivation frameworks: Self-Determination Theory, the Theory of Planned Behavior, the Transtheoretical Model of Change and positive reinforcement with social learning. Practical applications include letting the woman choose her activity, tracking progress, involving family, matching advice to her stage of change, and giving feedback. The aim is greater adherence and lower dropout.
points: Goals can target safety and prevention, functional optimization, metabolic and cardiovascular health, psychological well-being and childbirth preparation.
SMART means Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, for example improving the 30-s chair stand test from 10 to 14 repetitions.
Self-Determination Theory says behaviors last when the person feels autonomy, competence and relatedness.
Autonomy means choosing the activity (walking, swimming, prenatal yoga), while competence comes from achievable goals recorded in a tracking table.
The Theory of Planned Behavior links intention to attitudes, social support and perceived control, so educate, involve partner or family, and teach safe progression with RPE.
The Transtheoretical Model has five stages: precontemplation, contemplation, preparation, action and maintenance, each with matched interventions.
An action-stage example is a 30-min aerobic plus strength program started twice a week, with progress recorded.
Positive reinforcement includes feedback, group programs and tracking, such as a woman improving from 8 to 10 squats in 40 s and getting a new goal of 12.
Progression should be monitored with functional tests and RPE, adjusting intensity to the trimester.
takeaways: Write SMART goals with a measurable number and a deadline, such as before the third trimester.
Choose activities you enjoy and can adapt to your comfort level.
Keep a tracking table of repetitions, distance or RPE to see progress.
Bring partner, family or a group into your routine for support.
Find out which stage of change you are in and ask for matching support.
Ask your professional to adjust goals with feedback as you improve and as the trimester changes.
